## **Summary**

This report presents the combined results of two years of base-line investigations of birds performed during August 1999 - April 2001 in relation to the proposed construction of an offshore wind farm at Horns Rev in the Danish part of the North Sea ca 14 km southwest of Blåvandshuk.

Based on the distribution of the most abundant bird species recorded during 13 aerial surveys, there were no indications that the wind farm area was of any particular importance to the birds’ exploitation of the Horns Rev area. Fish-eating species like divers, gannet, terns, auks and gulls generally showed scattered and variable distributions, occurring in the areas north and south of Horns Rev, and with low numbers occurring on the reef proper and within the planned wind farm area. The distribution of benthic foraging species, eider and common scoter, showed that they mainly exploited the coastal parts of the area off Blåvandshuk and Skallingen, although the common scoter was found in relatively high numbers on the southeast slopes of Horns Rev

and within the wind farm area in the April 2001 survey.

Preference analyses of bird exploitation of the Horns Rev area showed that if the birds completely avoid the wind farm area after erection of the wind turbines, this will affects less than 1% of the different species, except divers of which 1.65% will be affected. If the birds avoid the wind farm area and an adjacent 4 km zone (worst case scenario), it is estimated to affect 11% of the common scoter, 10% of the gannet, 7-9% of the divers, alcids and velvet scoter and 0-6% of the remaining species.

The seasonal occurrence of the recorded species was fully comparable to the seasonal occurrence of these species recorded at Blåvandshuk since 1963. Year-to-year variation in abundance between the seasons August 1999 - April 2000 and August 2000 -April 2001 was mainly found in species that migrate through the Horns Rev area (terns, gannet, kittiwake), and with less pronounced variation in staging and wintering species (divers, herring gull, common scoter).

In granting permission to establish a wind farm at Horns Rev a number of conditions were laid down. These included programmes for establishing the environmental impacts of the construction of the wind farm and the following initial phase of operation. Particular emphasis was placed on the effects on birds species (migrating, staging and wintering) using the area, and, through specific studies, impact assessment analyses were to be provided for these species.

In their capacity as contractors for the planned wind farm, Elsamprojekt A/S (today Tech-wise A/S) prepared an EIA-report supplemented by technical background reports including the NERI bird report (Noer et al. 2000).

The NERI bird report described bird numbers and distributions in the Horns Rev area based on counts carried out during April 1999 - April 2000. In order to provide a well-founded base-

line material the counts were continued regularly during 2000 until April 2001.

The objectives of the counts were to obtain data that enable comparisons between the expected impact zone around the wind farm and a 'reference area', and to obtain data on which assessment of the relative importance of the entire area for birds can be made. The main purposes of the counts were to:

1. Map the numbers and distributions of birds in the area throughout the year, and

2. Assess the relative densities and numbers of the different species present.

This report presents the results of the counts from the period August 2000 - April 2001 and makes comparisons with the earlier results. For a more detailed description of the scope for the bird studies and the methods used see Noer et al. (2000).

## **2.1 Aerial surveys**

Mapping of bird distributions followed the method applied during the 1999-2000 surveys. Data on bird numbers and distribution were obtained from a total of six aerial surveys during August 2000 to April 2001 (Table 1). The study area, approximately 1,700 km[2] (38 x 52 km excluding the land area at Blåvandshuk), comprises the wind farm area (27.5 km[2] ) and the surrounding area which is referred to as the reference area. The study area was covered by a total of 26 north-south oriented, parallel transects, flown at 2 km intervals from Skallingen in the east, westwards to a line 37 km off Blåvandshuk (Fig. 1). Military activity prevented full coverage of the north-eastern part of the reference area on some surveys. Varying transect length is a result of temporary discontinuations of observations during periods of severe glare.

## **2.4 Assessment of potential disturbance effects**

To quantify and assess the importance of the wind farm area to birds, Jacob’s selectivity in-

dex (D) (Jacobs 1974) was calculated to describe the birds preference for the wind farm area compared to the surrounding reference area. The index (D), ranging from -1 (no birds in the wind farm area) to +1 (all birds in the wind farm area), can be tested by means of a one-sample χ[2] -test. The underlying assumption is that birds show a 'geographically free' distribution, which means that the birds are equally distributed throughout the survey area (D = 0). Indexes were also calculated for the wind farm area plus an adjacent 2 and 4 km zone, respectively (see Fig. 1).

In February 2001, the divers showed a very widespread and scattered distribution over the entire reference area, while in March 2001 the birds were located north and south of the Horns Rev, with relatively few birds in the central parts of the study area.

For the two periods investigated, the seasonal and year-to-year occurrences were very consistent (Fig. 2). Divers were recorded in the smallest numbers during autumn and in the highest numbers during late winter and spring. The numbers peaked in February and decreased during March and April.

## _Red-necked grebe, Podiceps griseigena_

One red-necked grebe was recorded (August 2000). Combined with previous observations (from the ship survey) of three birds (Noer et al. 2000), there are still no indications in the present material that the waters around Horns Rev are of ecological importance for the species.

## _Gannet, Sula bassanus_

A total of 136 gannets was recorded. The highest numbers were observed in August and October 2000 and in late April 2001. The phenological pattern matches the earlier findings (Noer et al. 2000). Gannets were generally recorded as solitary or in loose groups. In August 2000, the gannets occurred scattered throughout the reference area, while in April 2001, birds were only recorded west of the proposed wind farm area, with most birds located on the reef proper.

The seasonal occurrence of gannets (Fig. 4) reflects the peak migration periods (August-September, April-May). The highest numbers were observed during autumn migration in September. Analyses of the between-year variation are, however, constrained by the lack of a count in September 2000.

The distribution of all 442 gannets recorded during August 1999 - April 2001 is shown in Figure 5. There was a tendency for the highest numbers to be found off Blåvandshuk and in the western parts of Horns Rev.

## _Arctic/common tern, Sterna paradisaea/hirundo_

A total of 217 arctic/common terns was recorded. The species were only observed in August 2000 and April 2001, consistent with earlier findings. In both counts, the birds were recorded rather scattered throughout the area, although the majority of the birds in August 2000 were observed in the area off Blåvandshuk.

The seasonal occurrence of arctic/common terns reflects the peak migration periods in autumn (July-September) and spring (April-May; Fig. 6). Large between-year variation is evident, with the lowest numbers recorded in 2000/2001 and the highest numbers in 1999/2000.

The distribution of all 1,560 arctic/common terns recorded during August 1999 - April 2001 showed a scattered occurrence over the entire study area with a tendency of highest numbers in the area

off Blåvandshuk and Skallingen and in the area west of the proposed wind farm (Fig. 7).

## _Sandwich tern, Sterna sandvicensis_

A total of 298 sandwich terns was recorded. The species was only observed in August 2000 and April 2001. The highest numbers were observed in April, while in the previous year most records were made in August.

The seasonal occurrence of sandwich tern reflects the peak autumn (July-November) and spring (March-May) migration periods (Fig. 8). The April counts document large year-to-year variation.

## _Guillemot/razorbill, Uria aalge/Alca torda_

A total of 334 alcids was recorded with highest numbers recorded in October 2000. As previously observed (Noer et al. 2000), the birds were during all surveys mostly recorded singly or in small groups primarily in the western half of the reference area.

The seasonal occurrence of alcids showed the largest numbers during autumn (October-November) and the smallest numbers during winter and spring (Fig. 10). Although constrained by the different timing of the autumn counts during the two study periods, the year-to-year pattern of the occurrence compliment each other.

## _Herring gull, Larus argentatus_

A total of 4,905 herring gulls was recorded. The highest numbers were observed in March and April 2001, and the lowest numbers during autumn and winter. This differs from the previous observations through 1999/2000 (Noer et al. 2000), where most herring gulls were recorded during late winter and fewest during autumn and spring. In March-April 2001 most birds were recorded in the south-eastern parts of the study area, south of Blåvandshuk/Skallingen and off the Wadden Sea as observed in the 1999/2000 counts. The gulls often gather around fishing vessels and in the tidal zone during low tide.

## _Great black-backed gull, Larus marinus_

A total of 145 great black-backed gulls was recorded. The highest numbers were observed in August and October 2000 and in April 2001, where most birds were observed in the area off Blåvandshuk and in the southeastern parts of the reference area. As also recorded during the previous study period (Noer et al. 2000), the distributions of the species showed seasonal variation. However, in late autumn counts (October 2000 and November 1999) the distribution tended to be more offshore and less associated with the coastal parts of the area.

In February and April 2001, birds were found more concentrated on the northern slope of the reef and with few birds in the outermost western area.

The occurrence of kittiwakes showed substantial seasonal and year-to-year variation (Fig. 14). Despite large between-year variation, the main period of occurrence in the Horns Rev area was August-November, while only small numbers were recorded during late winter and spring.

The distribution of all 11,772 eiders recorded during August 1999 - April 2001 was very consistent. The species occurred in the coastal parts of the area off Blåvandshuk and Skallingen (Fig. 17). Only very few birds have been observed offshore on depths of more than 6 m.

## _Skuas, Stercorarius sp._

A total of 5 skuas were recorded (August 2000). The birds were not identified to species level, but were most likely Arctic skuas.

## **3.2.2 Species foraging on sessile benthic fauna**

## _Eider, Somateria mollissima_

A total of 8,441 eiders was recorded. The observations fully match the phenology and distributions recorded during the 1999/2000 surveys (Noer et al. 2000). The highest numbers were counted during winter and spring with a maximum in February 2001. Eiders were generally recorded in large flocks; solitary birds were only observed on a few occasions.

## _Common scoter, Melanitta nigra_

A total of 52,165 common scoters was recorded and was thus the most numerous species observed. The number of birds increased from August 2000 (283 birds) to April 2001 (16,902 birds). The distributions from December 2000 to March (Fig. 18a) were consistent with the distributions from the 1999/2000 period. In April 2001 the distribution was somewhat different from previous distributions with most birds found offshore at the south-east end of Horns Rev, further to the west than in the previous surveys, with only few birds in the area off Skallingen (Fig. 18b). In the latter count, a total of 2,482 individuals was recorded within the proposed wind farm area plus the adjacent 4-km zone, and 500 individuals within the proposed wind farm area itself.

The distribution of all 93,323 common scoters recorded during August 1999-April 2001 showed a consistent pattern (Fig. 20). The species mainly occurred in the area southwest and south of Blåvandshuk and in the area west of Fanø. ## **3.3 Disturbance effects**

In order to assess the magnitude of the potential disturbance effect on bird populations analyses of their exploitation of the proposed wind farm area and the adjacent areas were made in accordance with the methodology used in the previous investigation (Noer et al. 2000). These analyses included calculations of:

1. The percentage of birds within the wind farm area in relation to the number of birds in the total study area,

2. The percentage of birds within the wind farm area and an adjacent zone of 2 km in relation to the total number of birds in the study area,

3. The percentage of birds within the wind farm area and an adjacent zone of 4 km in relation to the total number of birds in the study area.

The adjacent 2 and 4 km zones are arbitrarily chosen and the latter (4 km zone) is considered as a 'worst case' scenario as the most conservative estimate of the area of potential habitat loss.

Within the proposed wind farm area, no species occurred in proportions higher than expected when assuming a 'geographical free' distribution in the study area. Most species, except divers, showed a significant avoidance of the wind farm area (i.e. they occurred in lower numbers than expected). Expanding the area with the adjacent 2-km zone provided a similar significant avoidance for all species, except divers. When the analyses included the adjacent 4-km zone, a significant positive preference was found for common scoter, while all other species, including divers but except gannet, still showed avoidance.

With small and mainly insignificant index values, the distribution of divers and alcids did not

deviate from what was expected from a 'geographical free' distribution. Thus, these species showed the most even distributions within the study area.

The calculated number of birds per survey kilometre in the wind farm area, in the area +2km and +4km are shown in Table 4. Compared to the number of birds per kilometre transect within the total reference area, an estimate of the relative importance of these areas to the different bird species can be obtained. In these calculations, the ratios between the number of birds recorded in the wind farm area and the number of birds recorded in the reference area should be equal to 1.0 if there was no preference for or avoidance of this area. ## **4.1 Within-year and betweenyear variation in bird numbers**

In order to make as precise assessments as possible of the potential impacts on birds from operating offshore wind farms, knowledge of the within-year and between-year variation in bird numbers is essential, both within the wind farm area as well as in the adjacent areas.

As the study period so far only comprises two years, it is difficult to assess whether the observed year-to-year variation in the abundance and the distribution of the species represent 'normal variation' in the Horns Rev area. In general bird numbers, of both migrating and wintering species may show large within-year and between-year fluctuations in abundance as well as in distribution. These variations may be related to factors such as reproductive success in the preceding breeding season, timing, duration and severity of winter, timing of spring, and availability of food resources.

The within-year variation in the occurrence of the bird species in the Horns Rev area closely correlate to the phenology of these species recorded at Blåvandshuk (Jacobsen in prep.). Thus, the present investigation did not find any deviation in the seasonal occurrence of the recorded species from what was expected.

The year-to-year variation in the abundance of the birds in the Horns Rev area was generally found in species that migrate through the area, e.g., terns, gannets and kittiwakes, while less pronounced variation was found in staging and wintering species, e.g. divers, gerring gulls and common scoters. Of the migrating species, both Arctic/common tern and sandwich tern have distinct migration periods (March-May and JulyAugust) and the timing and intensity of migration in these species may vary in relation to the weather conditions. Gannets have a short intense migration period in autumn (September),

and the recorded year-to-year variation in maximum occurrence of this species probably relate more to the difference in the timing of the counts during this period than to any real differences in abundance between years. Of the wintering species, only the Eider showed pronounced between-year variation in abundance in February.

## **4.2 Seabird use of the Horns Rev area**

From the spatial distributions of birds obtained during the two study periods (August 1999April 2000 and August 2000-April 2001), the following conclusions can be made.

Species foraging on fish (including gulls) were generally distributed in the offshore parts (more than ca 2 km from the coast) of the study area. The occurrence of these species was variable and all showed a more or less scattered distribution in the study area. During some counts, the highest numbers of, for example, gannets, alcids and kittiwakes, were observed north of Horns Rev, in other counts the highest numbers were observed south of Horns Rev. No species were found in high numbers on the shallow parts of Horns Rev (i.e. within the proposed wind farm area, _cf_ . Table 3 and 4).

Of species foraging on sessile benthic fauna (Eider and common scoter), only small numbers were observed at Horns Rev. The general distribution of these species is more coastal. In most cases the species were observed close to Blåvandshuk and Skallingen, although a relatively high number of common scoters were found exploiting the area southeast of Horns Rev in April 2001.

The data and calculations from the period August 1999 - April 2001 indicate a general tendency for lower than expected numbers within the wind farm area. Thus, it can be concluded that:

1. No data collected so far indicate that the wind farm area is of any particular importance to the birds’ exploitation of the Horns Rev area.

2. If the birds avoid exploiting the wind farm area, this will affect a maximum of 1% of the study area.

3. If the birds avoid the wind farm area the impact is estimated to affect less than 1% of the different species except divers of which 1.65% may be affected ( _cf_ . Table 3).

4. Even if a very conservative 'worst possible case' scenario is assumed, with birds totally avoiding the wind farm area and the adjacent 4 km zone the impact is estimated to affect ca 11% of the common scoters, ca 10% of the gannets, 7-9% of the divers, alcids and

velvet scoters, while the corresponding proportions of the remaining species will range within 0-6% ( _cf_ . Table 3).

These conclusions are in agreement with the conclusions based on the data from August 1999April 2000 (Noer et al. 2000), except for common scoter. The occurrence of this species showed a distinct change in distribution in April 2001 that involved more birds in the vicinity of the wind farm. Despite this change, the data indicate that the bird distributions are relatively consistent when considering both the withinyear and the between-year variation in abundance and distribution of the different species.
